title: Balarama Slays the Demon Balvala
story:
The morning of the parvan — the day that closed one cycle of the sages' rites — rose clear over the forest of Naimisha, where a great sacrifice had been running season after season, and the sages fed their fire and offered the day's oblations as they had done a hundred times before. Then, without warning, the sky above the sacrificial hall turned dark — not with cloud, but with a shape. From that darkness a rain began to fall, hissing into the fire and soiling the offerings: a rain of filth and impurity. The demon Balvala had come again.

It was exactly what the sages had described when they set the penance of Balarama — Krishna's elder brother, who had come to Naimisha as a pilgrim and, in a flash of anger, struck down their suta Romaharshana with one blade of grass. The demon was the son of Ilvala, cruel and ancient, a rover of the sky who at every parvan descended to defile their sacrifice at the very moment of its completion. For years they had endured him, powerless, watching their rites broken time and again by a hand they could not reach — the fire smothered, the offerings spoiled, the work of penance undone and begun again. And now they had in their midst the man whose penance was this demon's end. Every eye in the grove turned to Balarama, and he understood at once: this was the first half of his atonement, coming to meet him.

He saw the demon clearly — a body huge and black, like a mountain of crushed collyrium, drifting over the enclosure while the defilement rained down from him. And at the sight Balarama remembered his weapons, the plough and the mace that had torn apart the armies of the demons, and he did not wait. He raised the plough, and with its tip he caught the sky-roaming Balvala and dragged him down out of the air, and the demon fell to the earth before the fire. Balarama finished the work with his mace, and the defiler of Naimisha lay still at last, and the rain of impurity stopped as suddenly as it had begun.

The grove filled with the sages' joy, and it was a joy with years of helplessness behind it. They crowded around Balarama, praising him and calling down blessings that never fail; they laid upon him the vaijayanti, the celestial garland strung with lotuses that do not fade, and gave him garments from heaven itself. The fire that had been defiled so many times burned clean and bright above the demon's body, and the sacrifice went on as it had always been meant to go on.

With the sages' leave, Balarama set out from Naimisha the next morning, walking with the brahmanas, the priest-sages of the rite, toward the river Kaushiki — the first steps of the twelve-month pilgrimage that would carry him through all the holy fords of Bharatavarsha, the sacred land. The demon was dead. The penance had begun.
reflection: There is a strange economy in the episode: the same hands that committed brahma-hatya at Naimisha are the hands that free the sages' sacrifice, as if the penance and the service were one act. The sages' gift of the unfading garland and their unfailing blessings suggest that in their eyes the cleansing had already begun with the deed.
content_note: Demon-slaying: Balvala is dragged from the sky by the plough and his skull is crushed by the mace; described without graphic detail.
